comment: FYI: default dust threshold is 546 for P2PKH transactions, not 543.
parent_comment: Counterparty is a protocol built on top of the Bitcoin protocol. It allows you to issue, send, and trade "assets" on the blockchain. It does this by defining a set of message types (ex: issue, send) that can be encoded into bitcoin transactions. The Bitcoin blockchain is monitored for these messages and they are indexed and evaluated by federated nodes which come to consensus on which assets are issued, how many "tokens" they have, which addresses have what balances, etc. So, here's what a Counterparty transaction "looks like" (not really): ISSUE ASSET To: 1CounterpartyXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXUWLpVr Send: 0.00000543 BTC Fee: 0.0001 BTC Encoded: {"Create": ASSET, "Quantity": 10000000} SEND ASSET FROM: 1CounterpartyXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXUWLpVr TO: Some bitcoin address Send: 0.00000543 BTC Fee: 0.0001 BTC Encoded: {"Send": 10000 ASSET} In this example, I create an asset and then send some quantity of that asset. It's made possible by sending the minimum amount of bitcoin possible, paying the miner's fee, and encoding the Counterparty transaction data inside. Bitcoin is programmable money. This makes Bitcoin our data store, and bitcoin transactions our "save" function. Counterparty federated servers evaluate that data for validity and determine the current state of the network. To some people, it's controversial as it adds "weight" to the chain, it also bloats the UTXO pool, if you don't sweep the "dust" you create, but I see it as extending Bitcoin's functionality. Some cool features include: - Issuing dividends - Voting - Decentralized exchange

It's *probably* possible to calculate an expected value based on that, because of the assumption of the time window. Are there some standard measures of liquidity risk, and if so, how are they used?

parent_comment: Viability of outperforming the total market (indexing) over the long run? Hello all, So I am here to discuss the viability of my portfolio(s) (primarily roth ira at this moment) outperforming the total market (vti, vtsax, fstvx, however you want to measure it) over the span of ~35-40 years (retirement time). Just some basic information, 24 years of age, ~40k income, with student debt (not the topic at hand though). I also plan on getting a new job, shooting for at least ~50k in the next few months as my position now is primarily for getting me on my feet and some stability. Currently my portfolio consists of Fidelity Biotech fund - FBIOX - $2600 Berkshire Hathaway class B - BRK.B - $2900 I plan on fully funding it early around January - February for my 2015 contributions. I have a handful of stock picks in mind, primarily companies that have been around for a while and I truly do not expect them to go away. *insert Kodak, GE* comment here. I do understand the risks that I'm incurring but really is it that bad? On to the list of picks, Nike - NKE Chevron (and/or) Conocophillips - CVX - COP Philip Morris - PM So let me explain my reasoning for my current picks, and future picks as well as why I am not going all in the total market which would have been my alternative. FBIOX - Probably my riskiest choice as Biotech and healthcare in general can be and are extremely volatile. I do believe though over the long run this will continue to be profitable due to population growth and emerging markets requiring their products as well. BRK.B - My "safe" choice. It is basically a conglomerate and headed at the helm by Uncle Warren. Should he go down due to natural causes, could I be screwed? Potentially but most of his businesses run themselves anyways. Hopefully he will continue to go on to at least match Charlie Munger's age or even beyond. Regardless, I'd like to think that Berkshire can sustain its position and growth. NKE - Well I don't see them going anywhere but up to be honest. Nike is like the Coke of athletic apparel and will be the most sought after product in their industry. As emerging markets grow, they will have more money to spend on athletic apparel. It's not like many of these countries don't already love and play soccer (football) but they just don't have the nice shoes yet. Hopefully as they develop, they will generate lots of money for Nike and myself. Another pro I see for Nike is that unlike cars, houses, coke, purses *insert other consumer staple or discretionary good here*, is that it is easy to buy more than you need regarding athletic apparel. For most consumers, one car, one house and one (or two) cans of coke and a bottle of PG shampoo is enough. But when it comes to shoes? Well you can have one for each sport, then one for casual use then maybe a couple extra colors in each shoe if you so desire. Not to mention other cash cows like Elite socks which I think is ridiculous in that people pay full price for them. Disclosure, I own some that I purchased half off. Also in that they are such cash cows. Under Armour was a (barely) slight alternative but I don't think that it will have the sustainable growth that NKE does, although I do see them continuing to grow profitably for some time. Chevron / Conocophillips - Oil and gas won't be going away anytime soon but if it were to, I suspect that these large players will have their hands in the cookie jar and could just buy out any small competitors should that time come. My alternative here is Exxonmobil (XOM) but I'm chasing growth and I feel like XOM has less of it than these current choices. Chevron is a bit safer than Conocophillips but at the same time it's not doing too hot right now. I am between the two of these so either I will choose both or Chevron if I had to choose one. I just don't want to pay that transaction fee if I get both. Overall the industry has not been performing well and due to increased supply thus lower crude oil prices, they have not seen much growth recently. Fortunately I think that just means that these stocks (oil in general) are at a very good price right now. Phillip Morris - Like big oil, I do not see tobacco going anywhere either. Although smoking in the US has been declining, it's doing alright everywhere else in the world and hopefully will not go away anytime soon. Before PM was split off, it was a part of Altria Group (MO) which is probably one of the single best stocks you could have owned to date. I am choosing PM over MO because I'm more interested in the international growth. I do think they will both be good and MO may get a spot somewhere in my portfolio in the future but just not now. As you can probably already tell, I'm choosing relatively safe, well known companies with histories of success. Of course though, past performance is not an indicator of future returns. The environment for many of these companies are changing in ways that could truly cause them to be less profitable in the future relative to past returns ie. renewable energy, health concerns regarding tobacco, plain packaging. But I suppose there are always hurdles to jump over, they just change their face. I will also mention that I'm not interested in bonds whatsoever and should a market downturn come... well so be it. My retirement portfolio is ideally buy and hold forever thus I will be reinvesting my dividends here. I will probably build up a small taxable portfolio as well just for liquidity's sake and cause I'm a greedy bastard despite not being able to fully fund my 401k. Again, this is primarily for liquidity and I don't really know how much I will put in it so it may just be all cash waiting for an opportune time which is fine by me. I do plan on putting whatever I can into my HSA and 401k (not matched) within reason and will most likely just choose the total market fund or s&p 500 (whichever is available) when I start my new job.
